name: Cataract Canyon
reach: Potash to North Wash and Hite

camps.name: Little Bridge
camps.desc: Named in trip reports, in Meander Canyon above the confluence.

camps.name: Upper Lathrop Ledges
camps.desc: Above Lathrop Canyon. River trips may not camp at Lathrop Canyon itself, where the road ends.

camps.name: Indian Creek Camp
camps.desc: At the mouth of Indian Creek, with ruins nearby. Reports mention a waterfall hike up the creek in May and June.

camps.name: Upper Loop
camps.desc: At The Loop, where the river nearly doubles back on itself.

camps.name: Confluence
camps.desc: A big camp at the meeting of the Green and Colorado, well suited to a large group. Sometimes called the center of the universe.

camps.name: Lower Red Lake
camps.desc: Near Lower Red Lake Canyon, which has a trail to the Needles District.

camps.name: Upper Spanish Bottom
camps.desc: Above the first rapid. A large camp and a base for the Dollhouse trail.

camps.name: Middle Spanish Bottom
camps.desc: Above the first rapid. Big cottonwoods give shade for a kitchen and the Dollhouse trail starts close by. The landing can be steep at low water. From here you can walk the river trail down to Brown Bettie beach to see whether it is free.

camps.name: Brown Bettie beach
camps.desc: Below Rapid 1, with a trail upstream to the Dollhouse. A good beach at low water. Boats have to cheat right at Rapid 1 to make the eddy.

camps.name: Upper X/Y Canyon
camps.desc: Between Rapids 9 and 10.

camps.name: Middle X/Y Canyon
camps.desc: At the top of Rapid 10.

camps.name: Lower X/Y Canyon
camps.desc: Beside the Rapid 10 surf wave.

camps.name: Lake Cataract
camps.desc: A river-left camp in the quiet stretch between Rapid 12 and Range Canyon, a breather in the middle of the rapids. The eddy near shore is a good spot for a swim. Position approximate.

camps.name: Big Drop Beach
camps.desc: A river-left beach above the Big Drops and the usual high-water scouting point. Loud, and a hard place to sleep so close to the roar. At low water, scout from the river-left eddy above Big Drop 2 instead. Position approximate.

camps.name: Upper Ten Cent
camps.desc: A good river-left camp below the main rapids. Imperial Rapid and the rapids below it are still ahead before the lake. Position approximate.

camps.name: Lower Ten Cent
camps.desc: A large camp with a good landing. Position approximate.

camps.name: Imperial Camp
camps.desc: The last camp within the rapids, and a great high-water camp. The low-water landing is tricky: the 2011 flood took the beach, leaving a scramble over rocks or a tie-off in the current. Position approximate.

camps.name: Gypsum
camps.desc: A large, silt-free beach below the rapids.

camps.name: Clearwater Canyon
camps.desc: Named in trip reports.

camps.name: Millie Crag
camps.desc: Near Millie Crag Bend.

rapids.name: Rapid 1 (Brown Bettie)
rapids.desc: Hole in the center at low water; an easy line right.

rapids.name: Rapid 2
rapids.desc: Rocks left at low water; go center-right.

rapids.name: Rapid 3
rapids.desc: Straightforward, center-right.

rapids.name: Rapid 4
rapids.desc: Long, with rocks right at low water.

rapids.name: Rapid 5 (Surprise)
rapids.desc: A hidden hole left at low water and pour-overs on the right.

rapids.name: Rapid 6
rapids.desc: Big rocks right at low water; a good line left.

rapids.name: Rapid 7
rapids.desc: Also called North Seas. Longer and straightforward; follow the main current.

rapids.name: Rapid 8
rapids.desc: Options. Rocks at low water, a wall at the bottom right; the right side is good.

rapids.name: Rapid 9
rapids.desc: Easy, down the middle.

rapids.name: Rapid 10
rapids.desc: A big low-water wave: a surf for kayaks, a hit for rafts.

rapids.name: Rapid 11
rapids.desc: An inconsequential riffle.

rapids.name: Rapid 12
rapids.desc: The channel is constrained by debris from a river-left side canyon.

rapids.name: Rapid 13
rapids.desc: Outwash from Range Canyon. The start of about 3 miles of whitewater, the Mile Long Rapids (13 to 18).

rapids.name: Rapid 14
rapids.desc: A hole in the center, also Range Canyon outwash. Part of the Mile Long Rapids.

rapids.name: Rapid 15 (Capsize)
rapids.desc: Midstream boulders; line center-right. Inscriptions on river right mark the 1891 Best party's lost boat. Part of the Mile Long Rapids. A popular stop to scout and photograph.

rapids.name: Rapid 16
rapids.desc: A midstream boulder at low water. Part of the Mile Long Rapids.

rapids.name: Rapid 17
rapids.desc: Easy, down the middle. Part of the Mile Long Rapids.

rapids.name: Rapid 18
rapids.desc: Fun waves and hydraulics. Part of the Mile Long Rapids.

rapids.name: The Button (Rapid 19)
rapids.desc: A very large center hole at 35,000 cfs and up; a mid-river rock and wave hole left at low water.

rapids.name: Ben Hurt (Rapid 20)
rapids.desc: The river splits around an island; take the river-right channel.

rapids.name: Big Drop 1 (Rapid 21)
rapids.desc: The start of the main whitewater. Most pull out left at high water to scout.

rapids.name: Big Drop 2 (Rapid 22)
rapids.desc: A ledge wave, marked by a very large rock just left of center with more rocks below it, some with pillows that can flip a boat. Scout river left. At low water there are two lines: far right, with a hard pull left to miss a pin rock, or just left of the big rock, watching for a sleeper rock as you work right to left away from the rocky left bank. Left to right is preferred below 40,000 cfs. Boats 18 feet and under are reported fine on a clean line down to about 2,500 cfs. At high water the hole called Little Niagara is the thing to avoid.

rapids.name: Big Drop 3, Satan's Gut (Rapid 23)
rapids.desc: The biggest rapid, and a mandatory scout. The drop is steep enough to be striking when you look back up from below. At high water run right and stay off the left side. At flows down to about 2,500 cfs there is essentially one line: about 15 feet off the left bank, through an entry gap of roughly 10 to 15 feet, flushing you between the rock that forms Satan’s Gut on the left and another on the right, into a channel 15 to 20 feet wide. Missing the entry either way goes wrong quickly. Scout from the right-bank beach at high water and from the left-bank rocks at low water.

rapids.name: Rapid 24
rapids.desc: Read and run, down the middle.

rapids.name: Rapid 25
rapids.desc: Also called Repeat Rapid. Read and run, down the middle.

rapids.name: Ten Cent Rapid (Rapid 26)
rapids.desc: A midstream island; take the right channel.

rapids.name: Imperial Rapid (Rapid 27)
rapids.desc: Long, with big waves at the bottom. The first significant Lake Powell sediment deposits.

rapids.name: Short Rapid
rapids.desc: The narrowest part of the canyon; waves down the middle.

rapids.name: The Chute
rapids.desc: Easy; carved from sediment between 2007 and 2012.

rapids.name: Water Hole Canyon Rapid
rapids.desc: A wave hole center-right.

rapids.name: Can Opener Rapid
rapids.desc: Named for the tower on river left.

rapids.name: Benchmark Riffle
rapids.desc: Near a USGS benchmark.

rapids.name: La Rue's Riffle
rapids.desc: Straightforward.

rapids.name: Gypsum Canyon Rapid
rapids.desc: Appeared as a riffle in 2018 and is now significant. Scout left. A large pour-over can form middle right.

hikes.name: Petrified wood
hikes.desc: A pullout with petrified wood and a rock diving board.

hikes.name: Gooseneck
hikes.desc: Hike across the neck of the meander; trip reports say it is faster than motoring around.

hikes.name: Lathrop Canyon ruins
hikes.desc: Ancestral Puebloan ruins at Lathrop Canyon, where the road from the rim ends.

hikes.name: Indian Creek ruins
hikes.desc: Ruins along the cliff walls up the creek. Reports mention a waterfall up the creek in May and June.

hikes.name: The Loop
hikes.desc: Walk across the neck and rejoin the river, passing ruins and panoramic views.

hikes.name: Lower Red Lake Canyon
hikes.desc: A hiking trail up to the Needles District.

hikes.name: Dollhouse trail
hikes.desc: A trail from Spanish Bottom to the Doll House formations in the Maze District. Hiking is limited to designated trails. Stay on the trail to limit erosion, and secure boats and food at the beach, because wind and animals will get into loose gear.

hikes.name: Dark Canyon
hikes.desc: A creek-bed hike to waterfalls and rock formations. A designated camp no longer exists here.

flows: High water runs from early May to late June and can exceed 100,000 cfs; the same rapids at 3,000 cfs are a very different river. Rocks and holes show at low flow; at high flow features drown and big-water runs get pushy. The Button forms a very large center hole at 35,000 cfs and up, and the Big Drops carry more risk above 40,000.

At about 3,500 cfs reports describe a Class III river with holes and mid-channel rocks at Big Drop 3. At about 5,000 cfs Big Drop 3 is Class IV with the rest mostly III. At 6,000 to 7,000 cfs, reports describe more and larger rapids below Big Drop 3 and Gypsum Canyon at least Class IV.

As the reservoir drops, rapids that were drowned begin to show, and Gypsum Canyon Rapid has become significant since 2018. Sediment (the Dominy Formation) buries other rapids, including Dark Canyon Rapid as of 2021.

Riverbrain lists a recommended range of about 3,500 cfs minimum to 50,000 cfs maximum, with the Big Drops and Satan’s Gut needing a scout at any flow. At the extremes the same rapids behave very differently; check the gauges and recent reports before launching.
history: The 1891 Best party lost a boat at what became Capsize Rapid. Their inscriptions are on river right.
A fire at an oil well near the Potash ramp spilled thousands of barrels of oil into the river over several months.
John Wesley Powell named Cataract Canyon in 1869 for the difficulty of its rapids. Nathaniel Galloway made numerous trips through the canyon in 1894.
Hite Marina is named for Cass Hite, a prospector who worked the river’s gold bars in the 1880s.
Glen Canyon Dam and the lake

When Glen Canyon Dam closed on September 13, 1963, the Colorado began backing up and Lake Powell began to fill, drowning the lower end of Cataract Canyon. When the lake falls, drowned rapids reappear.

Emery and Ellsworth Kolb painted “E.C. & E.L. Kolb Cat Camp 2 10-28-1911” on a rock in Cataract Canyon during their 1911 trip down the Green and Colorado. It sits between Big Drop 2 and Big Drop 3, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and is only above water at medium to low flows.
indigenous: Ancestral Puebloan farmers lived in and around Canyonlands for centuries, building granaries in the cliffs and ruins along the river, such as those at Lathrop Canyon and the Coffee Pot Ruin. The Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples are their descendants; Ute, Paiute and Navajo peoples also used this country.
geology: Where the Colorado runs through the Cataract rapids it cuts through the Honaker Trail Formation, dark gray fossil-bearing limestone laid down about 286 to 320 million years ago in shallow Pennsylvanian seas, forming ledges and slopes along the river. Beneath it lies the Paradox Formation, thick salt and gypsum that dissolves and flows slowly, which flexes and faults the layers above and makes the beds slump toward the river.
planning: From Potash it is about 47 miles of flatwater through Meander Canyon, past Dead Horse Point, with ruins, pictographs and side hikes; Lathrop Canyon reaches the White Rim Road. About four miles below the Green River confluence the rapids begin, and about 15 miles of whitewater follow. Below Imperial Canyon the river slows into the upper reaches of Lake Powell, and flatwater runs to the take-out.

How much you row or motor depends on the flow, the lake level and the wind. Many groups bring a motor for the flat sections above and below the rapids; some tie boats together and float through the night. It can be done without a motor, but check the flow, lake level and wind forecast first and set expectations to match.
The camps near the confluence put you within reach of the Doll House in the Maze. Stay on the designated trail, and stash boats and gear so wind and animals cannot get into food or other items.

rules.d: One approved Type I, III or V whitewater life jacket per person, plus one spare per ten people or one per boat, whichever is fewer. Inflatable life jackets are not allowed on Utah rivers.
Between the Green and Colorado confluence and the last active rapid, life jackets must be worn, on the torso and fastened. Children 12 and under wear them at all times on the river.
One readily accessible spare oar, paddle or motor per boat. One spare paddle per three canoes or kayaks.
One Type IV throw cushion per boat 16 feet or longer. Smaller boats may carry a throw bag with at least 40 feet of line.
A repair kit and air pump for inflatables, a bailing device or bilge pump for boats that are not self-bailing, and a first-aid kit adequate for the group.
A rigid, durable metal fire pan large enough to hold all ash and debris. Turkey basting pans are not allowed.
A reusable, washable container with RV dump fittings, or a commercial bag system, stored in a hard-sided container or heavy-duty waterproof bag labelled "Human Waste". Pack all waste out.
A group on one permit travels and camps together and occupies only one campsite.
Do not camp within 300 feet of springs, intermittent streams, or archeological and historic sites. Do not use soap within 100 feet of springs or streams.
River trips may not camp at Lathrop Canyon, or at designated vehicle campsites on White Rim Road or in the Maze, unless the permit allows it.
Collect only driftwood below the high-water mark. Dead and down wood does not count. Fires stay in the fire pan, and all ash is packed out. Fire blankets are recommended.
Pets, firearms discharge, fireworks, personal watercraft, towing people behind boats, littering, and collecting or disturbing fossils, plants and rocks.
Traveling upstream between the first rapid in Cataract Canyon and Imperial Canyon is prohibited.

Salt Creek, Big Spring, Little Spring and Elephant Canyons (lower portions and mouths) are closed March 15 to September 1 for bighorn lambing. Jasper Canyon is closed above the first visible jump. The Doll House area is limited to designated trails.
Lower Red Lake Canyon to Cross and Y Canyons is day use only from December 1 to February 28, for bald eagles.

landmarks.name: Potash boat ramp
landmarks.desc: The usual put-in, near Moab. A potash mine just upstream makes fertilizer.

landmarks.name: Shafer oil well
landmarks.desc: Site of a 1925 oil fire that spilled thousands of barrels into the river over several months.

landmarks.name: Dead Horse Point
landmarks.desc: Horse thieves corralled stolen horses on the cliff-top, where they died of thirst.

landmarks.name: Coffee Pot Ruin
landmarks.desc: An Ancestral Puebloan granary built in a sandstone spire. Hard to reach but visible from the river.

landmarks.name: Salt Creek
landmarks.desc: The mouth is closed March 15 to September 1 for bighorn lambing, as are Big Spring, Little Spring and Elephant Canyons.

landmarks.name: Elephant Canyon
landmarks.desc: The mouth is closed March 15 to September 1 for bighorn lambing, along with Salt Creek, Big Spring and Little Spring.

landmarks.name: Green River confluence
landmarks.desc: The start of Cataract Canyon. Life jackets must be worn from here to the last active rapid. Up-running is prohibited from the first rapid to Imperial Canyon. A courtesy register box is a little below.

landmarks.name: Little Niagara
landmarks.desc: A large hole in Big Drop 2 that matters most at high water.

landmarks.name: Kolb Brothers inscription
landmarks.desc: Painted by Emery and Ellsworth Kolb at their Cat Camp in 1911, between Big Drop 2 and Big Drop 3. It is only above water at medium to low flows. Look, photograph, never touch.

landmarks.name: Imperial Canyon
landmarks.desc: The first significant Lake Powell sediment deposits (the Dominy Formation) start here.

landmarks.name: Dark Canyon Rapid
landmarks.desc: Once a top rapid; buried by Lake Powell sediment as of 2021.

landmarks.name: North Wash boat ramp
landmarks.desc: The usual take-out, on river right just below the Dirty Devil confluence. A steep, eroded ramp with mud flats and quicksand; a winch and rollers are often needed. Contact the NPS about conditions.

landmarks.name: Hite Marina boat ramp
landmarks.desc: River left. Usually high and dry unless the reservoir is full.

notes.camp: *River trips camp together on one site per permit. Do not camp at Lathrop Canyon, at springs, or near ruins. Cryptobiotic soil crust covers the benches: stay on rock, sand and wash bottoms.
notes.hike: *Hikes begin on side canyon washes that flash flood, and the heat is severe in summer. Ruins and rock art are fragile: look and photograph but never touch or remove anything.

access.name: Moab
access.note: Nearest town to Potash; the park office is here

access.name: Hanksville
access.note: Nearest town to North Wash and Hite

access.name: Potash
access.note: Put-in on the Colorado, reached from Moab

access.name: North Wash
access.note: Usual take-out, a dirt ramp just below the Dirty Devil. Steep and eroded, and how muddy it is varies, so bring a winch or rollers.

access.name: Hite Marina
access.note: Alternative take-out. A concrete ramp when the lake is high enough, with restrooms, water and a waste dump station; as muddy as North Wash when the lake is low. Camping is possible but poor, so land, de-rig and go.

permit.status: Required for overnight trips · reserve on Recreation.gov, no lottery

items.d: There is no lottery. Overnight river permits are reserved on Recreation.gov, up to four months before each season. Reservations close two days before the launch date.
Launches April 14 to October 15 open on December 14. Launches October 16 to April 13 open on June 15.

The permit is valid only within Canyonlands National Park, downstream of the Potash and Mineral Bottom boat ramps. If you launch upstream, the start date is the day you enter the park. Mineral Bottom trips on the Green River above that need a separate BLM permit (Labyrinth Canyon).
Day-use permits are separate and open up to 24 hours ahead.

River users must register for campsites below the confluence. Designated campsites are along the rivers; sandbars are usually plentiful in late summer and fall, but camps can be hard to find at high water.
Private trips need technical whitewater experience. Guided trips must use an NPS-authorized company.
$36 per permit, which includes the $6 Recreation.gov fee.
$25 per person for overnight Cataract Canyon and flatwater trips. Older pages say $20. Day use is $6 plus $10 per person. Fees are non-refundable.
Up to 40 people. Combined groups camping together may not exceed 40.
Up to 14 consecutive nights.
There are no daily launch limits in Canyonlands.
The usual take-out at Lake Powell is the North Wash ramp. It is steep and eroded, and a winch or rollers are often needed. Check lake levels and the take-out calendar with the park.
The Hite Marina ramp is usually high and dry. Bullfrog, about 48 river miles farther, is the alternative.
Mussels are in Lake Powell. Utah and Arizona laws require you to clean, drain and dry your boat after take-out.

stats.season: Year-round. Runoff peaks May to June; the permit season runs April to October.

flow.note: This is the combined Colorado and Green River flow below the confluence, which is what runs through the rapids. The Big Drops need a scout at any flow.

bands.label: Class III to IV
bands.d: Serious water. A flip can cost you loose gear.

bands.label: Class III to IV
bands.d: A real chance of a beating.

bands.label: Class IV+
bands.d: Big water. Long scouts at the big drops.
